n: Chapters 24–27 are often called Isaiah’s “little apocalypse,” describing God’s judgment on the whole earth before His reign. The Lord will empty the earth, turn it upside down, and scatter its people.
No one will be spared because of status: priest and people, master and servant, buyer and seller, lender and borrower — all face the same judgment.

f.w: as with the people, so with the priest

n: The land will be completely emptied and plundered, because the Lord has spoken.
The earth dries up and withers; the whole world wastes away, and even the proud powers of the earth weaken.

The earth is polluted by its people because they have broken God’s laws, twisted His ordinances, and broken the everlasting covenant. The Lord quotes this in D&C 1 to describe the latter-day apostasy.
So a curse consumes the earth; its people bear their guilt, are burned, and few remain. Latter-day scripture describes the earth being cleansed by fire at the Second Coming.
The new wine dries up, the vines wither, and those who were cheerful groan.
The happy sound of tambourines and harps stops; party noise falls silent.
People no longer drink with singing; even strong drink tastes bitter.
The “city of chaos” — a picture of the world’s organized wickedness — is broken down, and every house is barred shut.

f.g: Hebrew tohu — the same word for “without form” in Genesis 1:2; a city returned to chaos.

n: People cry in the streets for wine; all joy has turned to gloom and gladness is banished from the land.
Only ruin remains in the city, and its gate is battered to pieces.

f.g: The city gate — center of public life and defense.

n: Yet like the few olives left after a tree is beaten or grapes left after harvest, a remnant will survive.

f.w: the shaking of an olive tree

n: The survivors raise their voices and sing for joy about the Lord’s majesty, shouting from the west, across the sea.
So glorify the Lord in the east and honor His name in the islands of the sea. Latter-day Saints note that Israel was scattered to the “isles of the sea,” and praise will rise from there too.

f.g: Better “in the east” (the regions of light/dawn).

n: From the ends of the earth come songs praising the Righteous One. But Isaiah feels sick at heart: betrayers keep betraying. Joy and grief exist side by side until the end.

f.g: “I waste away!” — an expression of grief.

n: Terror, pit, and trap await the people of the earth. In Hebrew, the three words sound alike: pachad, pachat, pach.

f.w: Fear, and the pit, and the snare

n: Whoever escapes one danger falls into the next. The floodgates of heaven open, as in Noah’s day, and earth’s foundations shake.

f.w: the windows from on high are open
the foundations of the earth do shake

n: The earth is shattered, split apart, and violently shaken. The threefold repetition emphasizes total upheaval.
The earth staggers like a drunk and sways like a flimsy shelter. Its sin weighs it down; it falls and won’t rise again — the old world order ends.

f.w: reel to and fro like a drunkard

f.g: A flimsy hut or watchman’s shelter.

n: In that day the Lord will punish rebellious powers in heaven and the proud kings on earth — both spiritual and political evil.

f.w: the host of the high ones
f.g: Rebellious heavenly powers — spiritual forces of evil.

n: They will be gathered like prisoners in a pit and locked up, and after many days they will be “visited.” Latter-day Saints see in this the spirit prison and the gospel later being preached to the dead.

f.w: after many days shall they be visited

n: Then the moon will blush and the sun be ashamed, for the Lord’s glory will outshine them when He reigns gloriously in Mount Zion and Jerusalem before His elders. This points to Christ’s millennial reign.

f.w: the LORD of hosts shall reign in mount Zion

f.g: His elders — perhaps like the seventy elders who saw God at Sinai (Exodus 24:9-11).
